attempts.text: Agreement with human judgments, consistency across languages, and stability across repeated calls describe different aspects of an automated evaluator. A judge may produce stable decisions that are nevertheless incorrect, or agree with humans in one language but not on a meaning-matched version in another. We propose a controlled bilingual study that measures these properties separately in context-grounded short question answering. The feasibility pilot will contain 20 passage–question items, each with a correct and a deliberately incorrect answer in English and one additional language. Two fluent raters will independently assess each response before adjudication. One fixed language-model judge will evaluate the responses under English instructions, with an additional target-language instruction condition and three calls per condition. The analysis will separate human-reference agreement, cross-language decision changes, repeated-call stability, and non-decisions. The proposed contribution is a human-validated replication-and-extension protocol for a bounded QA setting; it does not claim to introduce multilingual judging. The study is designed to distinguish incorrect judgments from unstable judgments and data-construction problems; no direction of effect is assumed.
